About this citation

The aphorism numbers are the locator, and they are stable. Section 341 is the eternal-recurrence question; §276 is the line about wanting to learn nothing new anymore. The 1887 edition added a fifth book, so the year attached to an aphorism matters for which collection it sits in.

### Exact wording

English (as recorded here)

“This life as you now live it and have lived it, you will have to live once more and innumerable times more…”

German

“Dieses Leben, wie du es jetzt lebst und gelebt hast, wirst du noch einmal und noch unzählige Male leben müssen.”

The demon's speech in The Gay Science §341. The English rendering preserves the sentence break, which is what makes the passage overwhelming.

#### Forms in circulation that differ

-   “What if a demon told you this life would repeat endlessly?”
-   “Eternal recurrence.”

### Attribution notes

This is the thought experiment of the eternal recurrence — and in §341 it is a demon's speech whose purpose is a test, closing with the question of whether you could want it. Readers often present the recurrence as Nietzsche's cosmology, a claim about how the universe actually runs; in The Gay Science it is a condition posed to a single reader, and the later notes in which he took it more literally are a different and much cruder form of the idea.

#### About Friedrich Nietzsche

Friedrich Nietzsche (1844–1900) was a German classical philologist who became a radical critic of morality, metaphysics, and modern culture. Appointed professor at Basel at twenty-four, he resigned from ill health and wrote in solitude across Switzerland, Italy, and Germany.

### How to read this passage

Free will, decision theory, and existential choice all ask how choosing is possible and what makes a choice one’s own. This passage enters that discussion through choice, affirmation.
